answer.exemplar: Mean imputation writes the arithmetic mean of the observed values in that column, so every missing cell receives the same central value.

questions.explanation: The imputed value is the column's observed mean, applied uniformly.

questions.topic: How far the median fill sits below the mean
questions.stem: In a how far the median fill sits below the mean review, the logged values are 61 and 10. Explain what a large gap between median and mean indicates about a distribution.

answer.exemplar: A large gap indicates skew: the mean is pulled toward the tail, while the median stays at the center, revealing asymmetry in the data.

questions.explanation: A large median-mean gap signals skew: the mean is pulled toward a long tail while the median stays near the bulk. A roughly symmetric distribution has a small gap.

questions.topic: The share a mode fill creates
questions.stem: A worked the share a mode fill creates example uses the figures 62 and 11. Explain how mode imputation affects the frequency of the most common category.

answer.exemplar: Mode imputation adds every missing value to the most common category, inflating its share and potentially overstating its prevalence.

questions.explanation: Mode imputation assigns every missing entry to the most frequent category, so that category's count and share rise. Other categories gain nothing.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The cost of a blanket drop
questions.stem: A case study of the cost of a blanket drop supplies the data 63 and 12. Explain the main cost of dropping all rows with any missing value.

answer.exemplar: Blanket dropping can discard a large fraction of data and bias the sample if missingness is not completely random, reducing power and representativeness.

questions.explanation: Dropping rows wastes data and can bias results when missingness is systematic.
questions.hint: Dropping wastes data and risks bias.
